summary: This standard describes how IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies are encapsulated for transmission over FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network technology. It lets IP hosts and routers share an FDDI network.

eli5.summary: Different kinds of cables and networks need different envelopes for the same mail. This paper explains how to wrap Internet messages so they travel across a fiber-optic ring network.

questions: how to send ip over fddi
how does ip work over fddi
what is the mtu of fddi
how does arp work on fddi
subtitle: How IP datagrams and ARP messages are wrapped in LLC/SNAP so they can cross a fiber-optic FDDI ring, and still bridge to Ethernet.

tldr.problem: FDDI is a fiber-optic LAN with its own frame format and addresses, so IP hosts and routers need an agreed way to put datagrams and ARP messages on it that works the same on every implementation.
tldr.mechanism: IP and ARP packets ride inside IEEE 802.2 LLC Type 1 frames with a SNAP header carrying the EtherType. ARP maps 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses, and the MTU is fixed at 4352 octets.
tldr.outcome: Stations on FDDI can interoperate with each other and, through translational bridges, with Ethernet stations. This RFC is an Internet Standard (STD 36) and no newer RFC is recorded as replacing it.

today: RFC 1390 is an Internet Standard (STD 36), and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 1188 as the definition of IP and ARP over FDDI.

sections.title: Goal and Scope
sections.content:
The goal is compatible, interoperable implementations for sending IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies over FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface). FDDI standards cover the physical layer and the Media Access Control (MAC) sublayer of the data link layer. The rest of the data link service comes from the IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) service, so the stack is IP/ARP over 802.2 LLC over FDDI MAC, PHY and PMD.

The memo states an explicit intent: IP and ARP on FDDI stations must be able to interoperate with stations on Ethernet through translational bridges. It covers single MAC stations only (single-attach or dual-attach), not dual MAC stations. Much of the text is drawn from RFC 1042, which does the same job for IEEE 802 networks.
sections.eli5: The goal is to make sure every computer on the fiber ring wraps its Internet mail the same way, and that the mail can still pass to an Ethernet neighbor.

sections.title: Encapsulation in LLC and SNAP
sections.content:
Every IP datagram and ARP message sent on FDDI is encapsulated in an 802.2 LLC header and a SNAP (Sub-Network Access Protocol) header, inside the FDDI MAC frame. Only 802.2 LLC Type 1 is used, and every frame is sent as an Unnumbered Information frame.

The DSAP and SSAP fields are both set to 170, the control field is 3, and the 24-bit Organization Code in the SNAP header must be zero. The remaining 16 bits are the EtherType from Assigned Numbers: 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP. The LLC and SNAP headers together take 8 octets.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a small label on the front that says what is inside: an Internet letter or an address question. The label is always the same size, so everyone can find it.

sections.title: Address Resolution with ARP
sections.content:
Mapping a 32-bit Internet address to a 48-bit FDDI address is done with the dynamic discovery procedure of ARP (RFC 826). Each host must know its own Internet address, answer requests for it, and use ARP to translate other Internet addresses when needed.

The ARP fields are set as follows: the protocol type for IP is 2048, the hardware address length is 6, the protocol address length is 4, and the operation code is 1 for a request and 2 for a reply. The hardware type code assigned to IEEE 802 networks is 6 and the one for Ethernet is 1. Because differing values cause trouble in bridged environments, ARP packets are sent with hardware type 1 and are accepted when received with hardware type 1.

For the same bridging reason, the hardware addresses inside ARP packets must be in canonical bit order, with the Group bit as the low-order bit of the first octet. FDDI normally writes addresses with the Group bit in the high-order position, so each octet must be bit-reversed.
sections.eli5: To find out which mailbox belongs to an Internet address, a computer asks everyone on the ring. To stay compatible with Ethernet, it writes the answer using the Ethernet-style labels.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast
sections.content:
The broadcast Internet address, the one with a host part of all binary ones, must be mapped to the broadcast FDDI address of all binary ones.

If IP multicasting is supported on an FDDI network, the method in RFC 1112 is used. An IP multicast address maps to an FDDI group address by placing the low-order 23 bits of the IP address into the low-order 23 bits of the group address 01-00-5E-00-00-00 (in canonical order). For example, 224.255.0.2 maps to 01-00-5E-7F-00-02, which becomes 80-00-7A-FE-00-40 when bit-reversed for transmission in native order. Supporting multicast may require a station to copy frames addressed to any of an arbitrary number of group addresses.
sections.eli5: Shouting to everyone uses a special all-ones address. Talking to a club uses an address built from the club's number.

sections.title: Packet Size and the MTU
sections.content:
The FDDI MAC defines a maximum frame of 9000 symbols (4500 octets), which leaves roughly 4470 octets for data after the LLC/SNAP header. To leave room for future MAC header and frame status extensions, the MTU of FDDI networks is set at 4352 octets: 4096 octets of data and 256 octets of headers at the network layer and above. Implementations must not send packets larger than the MTU.

Gateways must accept packets as large as the MTU and fragment them when necessary, and should accept packets as large as a maximum size FDDI frame. Hosts should be prepared to accept packets as large as the MTU, but must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they know the destination will accept them. A host may state its preference in TCP using the Maximum Segment Size option. There is no minimum packet size on FDDI, and implementations must be prepared to receive and ignore trailing pad octets, to stay interoperable with Ethernet in a bridged environment.
sections.eli5: A box on the fiber ring can hold a lot, but the rule is to pack only up to a set size so there is always spare room. Small boxes are safest when sending far away.

sections.title: MAC and 802.2 Details
sections.content:
Only 48-bit addresses are used with IP and ARP, to avoid problems between 16-bit and 48-bit stations. All IP and ARP frames are sent as Asynchronous LLC frames using Unrestricted tokens. The priority is a local matter, and implementations should make it tunable. Receiving IP and ARP packets in Synchronous frames and Restricted Asynchronous frames is recommended. Hosts directly on FDDI must not use trailer encapsulations, and IP datagrams go out as big-endian 8-bit bytes. The Frame Copied and Address Recognized indicators may be used for decisions like link-level retransmission, but their meaning, especially with bridges, was not well defined at the time of writing.

Implementations must support 802.2 Class I service, which needs Unnumbered Information, XID and TEST frames. UI responses, and UI commands with the Poll bit set, are ignored. XID and TEST commands get a response only if the DSAP is the SNAP SAP (170), the Null SAP (0) or the Global SAP (255). XID responses carry the information field 129.1.0, and TEST responses echo the information field they received.
sections.eli5: There are also housekeeping rules, like which lane to use on the ring and how to answer a quick "are you there?" knock from a neighbor.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1188 and Security
sections.content:
This memo revises RFC 1188. A reference to a future dual-MAC document was removed, a statement of intent to support FDDI and Ethernet interoperability was added, and acceptance of ARP frames with hardware type code 6 (IEEE 802) was removed. The references and the author's address were also updated.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: This version fixes a few things from the older one, mainly so ring computers and Ethernet computers can talk. It does not say anything about keeping messages secret.

fields.name: DSAP
fields.desc: Destination service access point, set to the SNAP value.

fields.name: SSAP
fields.desc: Source service access point, set to the SNAP value.

fields.name: Org Code
fields.desc: SNAP organization code; must be zero.
